This video is going to look and sound a little
different from my usual content because this
topic is serious, complex, and infuriating.

It’s also incredibly long, as you’ve probably
noticed, but it is necessary to understand
the full picture.

As we’re going through this story, I want
you to keep this one simple question in the

back of your mind – When was the last slave
freed in America?
1865, at the end of the Civil War.

Everyone knows that, that’s probably the
second easiest elementary school history question
I could possibly think of.
Well…

Well, okay, if you want to get technical about
it, it was after the 13th Amendment, which
was a few months after the war ended.
Eh…

Is this some kind of trick question where
you’re going to claim something abstract

like shift work is actually a continuation
of slavery?
No [sighs], traditional chattel slavery.
[Snaps fingers] Juneteenth, final answer.
[Exasperated sigh] …Still wrong.

Is this going to be another hour-long Knowing
Better video about how something we thought
ended a century ago actually didn’t?
[Click of old TV turning on]
[Intro music]

This video was brought to you by CuriosityStream
and Nebula.

You’re telling me they invented a picture
frame that can show whatever image you want
on it?
Will you get back in the closet, man?

This really isn’t a topic for light-hearted
characters.

You’re talking about the Civil War and you
don’t need your Civil War character?

We’re actually going to be talking about
a whole lot more than just the Civil War.

But that’s irrelevant, nobody cares about
you, most people don’t even know your name.

And besides, if I use you, everyone’s just
going to say Atun-Shei did it better.
Checkmate, Lincolnites…
You’re right.

[Door slam]
Okay well, like the majority of my audience,
I’m an American…
always have been.

I went through elementary, middle, and high
school, then I went on to college to become

a Social Studies teacher, and then, I taught
US History in two different states at the
middle and high school level.

Am I giving you my credentials in order to
brag?
No, quite the opposite actually.

I was taught what I’m going to be calling
“the Standard American History Myth.”

Throughout all my years of education, including
college twice, the story had barely changed
between the 1990s and the 2010s.

And then I taught that same myth to the next
generation of students.

Since I’m going to be spending the rest
of this video dismantling this story, and

at least some of my audience isn’t American,
it’s probably a good idea to make sure we’re
all on the same page.

As you can see, I have a brand new… ish
TV, so I can show you video clips whenever
I want.

Now, I found this video from an online university
that sums up what most of us have been taught

and therefore believe about American history…
lemme just…

[TV static]
US History in four minutes or less.

America was founded when a group of Protestant
Christians, fleeing religious persecution

in Europe, made the harrowing journey across
the Atlantic Ocean and landed at Plymouth
Rock.

These Pilgrims had a feast with the Indians
to celebrate their cooperation and that became
the holiday of Thanksgiving.

Over the next few decades, several other British
colonies were founded on the American continent

and in 1776 they all declared their independence
from the King over the issue of taxation without
representation.

After the Revolutionary War had been won,
the founding fathers wrote the Constitution,

a freedom-loving liberty document which guaranteed
that all men were created equal.

There’s one glaring hypocrisy with that
statement, though – the fact that slavery
existed in America.

How could the founding fathers believe in
equality while many of them were also slaveowners?

Well, many of them knew that this peculiar
institution was morally wrong and thought

that the practice would naturally die out
on its own, but just to be sure, they put

a clause in the Constitution saying that the
importation of new slaves would end in 1808.

None of the founding fathers could have predicted
the cotton gin though, which suddenly made

slavery much more profitable and all but guaranteed
it would continue for another century.

Throughout the 1800s, abolitionists like Frederick
Douglass fought to end the practice and in

1860, Abraham Lincoln was elected on that
very platform.

In order to protect their rights as states
and keep their taxes from increasing, several

Southern states decided to break away from
the Union and form their own country known
as the Confederacy.

From 1861 to 1865, America fought the bloodiest
war in its history and in the end, the Union

was preserved, and 4 million black people
were freed from bondage.

It's a common misconception that Abraham Lincoln
freed the slaves, but the Emancipation Proclamation

only applied to areas in active rebellion,
meaning the Confederate States.

There was no way to enforce that without invading
and the Northern slave states were unaffected,
so this didn’t really do much.

In reality, it wasn’t the Great Emancipator,
but the 13th Amendment, ratified eight months
after his assassination, that abolished slavery.

Reconstruction lasted from 1865 to 1877 and
was marked by a period of relative peace since

federal troops were stationed in the South
to guarantee the rights of the recently freed
slaves.

After Reconstruction ended though, things
got pretty dark pretty fast.

Within a decade, Black Codes had been passed
in every Southern state and many of them required
literacy tests and poll taxes to vote.

This is the beginning of Jim Crow, an era
where black people had to sit at the back

of the bus and drink out of separate water
fountains, they even had separate schools
for white kids and black kids.

That lasted until 1954 when the Supreme Court
decided to desegregate public schools with
the Brown v. Board of Education decision.

This began the Civil Rights movement, which
gave rise to leaders like Martin Luther King

who said we should judge each other not by
the color of our skin, but by the content
of our character.

With the passage of the Civil Rights Act of
1964, Jim Crow and segregation were over,

and America had finally swept away the last
vestiges of racism in the country.
We even elected a black man as president – twice.

So, the next time someone tells you that America
is a racist country with racism in our DNA,
hopefully now, you’ll know better.

I’m Knowless Better, author of “You Learned
Everything You Need to Know About History
in Elementary School” for Better University.

Thank you for watching, to help keep Knowing
Better videos free, subscribe to our Patreon

page at patr–
[TV static]

I don’t apologize for that, nor do you actually
want an apology… that was hilarious.

You’re probably familiar with most of what

for the most part, that was the story you

believe.

It’s also the story fake Youtube universities
continue to push to this day.

Yes, that was a PragerU parody, just about

And they’re usually pushing the message

I was spared the life sapping, negative messages
about America that are crippling a generation

These ideas are poison.

As a Social Studies teacher, I can assure

America is a racist country or was founded

And they’re certainly not learning Critical
Race Theory.

Because if you stray from that standard story,

And honestly, for years afterward.

But that general story, the standard myth
that America was founded on freedom, slavery

ended after the Civil War, and segregation
lasted until Martin Luther King, doesn’t

really explain the current state of racial
inequality and leaves a lot more questions

Why haven’t they “caught up yet?”

You can come at this from multiple different

Why do they perform worse in school?
Why do they make less money?
Why are they convicted of more crimes?

Why aren’t they elected to office at a rate
more proportion– [TV static] The point is,
you’re never given an answer to these questions.

You’re left to make it up on your own; if
America is the land of equality and some people

just can’t seem to do well, there must be
something inherently different about that

group of people specifically that prevents
them from succeeding.

Most Americans are never taught that maybe
the system itself is rigged against them.

But even more than that, they never learn
that the fundamental premise of that question

– that slavery ended 150 years ago – is
incorrect.

I’m not talking about the prison industrial
complex or unpaid internships; I’m talking
about ball-and-chain chattel slavery.

If the Standard American History Myth that
we all grew up hearing is wrong…
When was the last slave freed in America?

use to slave labor after a worker’s strike

This will be a recurring theme going forward,

Over the next two centuries, the rich white

And at this point, slavery was still legal

In 1769, Charles Stewart traveled with his

until Somerset tried to escape and was imprisoned.

In 1772, his case was heard by Lord Mansfield,
the Chief Justice of the King’s Bench, who

The state of slavery is of such a nature that

it is incapable of being introduced on any
reasons, moral or political, but only by positive
law.

… It is so odious, that nothing can be suffered

Whatever inconveniences, therefore, may follow
from the decision, I cannot say this case

is allowed or approved by the law of England;
and therefore the black must be discharged.

Basically, what he just said is that slavery
is an unnatural condition and can only exist

if there is a law specifically stating it

law.

There was no such law in England, therefore
slavery cannot exist there.

It’s unclear who came up with this famous
line, but it was said that the air in England

free.

This decision popularized the abolition and
anti-slavery movements, which had quietly
existed for some time.

You know the next part, there’s some spilled

A few years after that, the founding fathers
got together to write the Constitution.

There were fifty-five delegates, so there
were disagreements on nearly every issue,

among the noteworthy, there were abolitionists

Jefferson.

As a result, the issue of slavery appears
in the Constitution three times without ever
actually using the word “slavery.”
Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 states…

Representatives and direct Taxes shall be
apportioned among the several States which

may be included within this Union, according
to their respective Numbers, which shall be

determined by adding to the whole Number of
free Persons, including those bound to Service

for a Term of Years, and excluding Indians

This is the Three-Fifths Compromise, which
we all learn about in school.

Two things to note here, first, it doesn’t
say that black people are only worth three-fifths

is basically the same thing but worded slightly
differently.

Secondly, indentured servants still counted
towards the population, it was just Indians
and other persons who are not.

It wasn’t the racists of the South who wanted
to count slave populations less than white

populations – it was the abolitionists in
the North.

Not sure why it keeps cutting to stuff, these

That way, they could artificially inflate

Unlike in Britain, in America, breathing free
